title: AT 99 YEARS OLD, GOD STILL ASKED ABRAHAM TO CUT SOMETHING AWAY.
paragraphs: AT 99 YEARS OLD, GOD STILL ASKED ABRAHAM TO CUT SOMETHING AWAY.
You are never too old to surrender, too broken to be restored, or too far into your story for God to rewrite what comes next.
“Abraham was ninety-nine years old when he was circumcised.” — Genesis 17:24
Ninety-nine years old.
Let that sink in.
Most people would have considered his remaining years a time to rest, enjoy what he had accumulated, and settle comfortably into the life he had built.
But God was not finished with Abraham.
There was still something to surrender. Something to remove. Something that would permanently mark his relationship with God.
And perhaps that is precisely why this ancient passage should make some of us uncomfortable.

Because we want God to change our circumstances without changing our character. We want His promises without surrendering our preferences. We want resurrection without dying to ourselves. We want Him to bless the very things we refuse to place under His authority.
We want a Savior who comforts us, but sometimes resist the Lord who confronts us.
Abraham was ninety-nine when God required a deeply personal act of obedience.
What have you spent years refusing to surrender?
That bitterness you have learned to live with?
That secret addiction nobody knows about?
That relationship you know is pulling you away from Christ?
That pride you have disguised as self-respect?
That unforgiveness you have justified because someone genuinely wounded you?
Perhaps you have carried something for so long that you no longer recognize it as something that needs to change.
It has become familiar.
But familiarity does not make something holy.
Genesis 17:24–27 records:

“And Abraham was ninety years old and nine, when he was circumcised in the flesh of his foreskin. And Ishmael his son was thirteen years old, when he was circumcised in the flesh of his foreskin. In the selfsame day was Abraham circumcised, and Ishmael his son. And all the men of his house, born in the house, and bought with money of the stranger, were circumcised with him.” — KJV
The original Hebrew of Genesis 17:24 reads:
וְאַבְרָהָם בֶּן־תִּשְׁעִים וָתֵשַׁע שָׁנָה בְּהִמֹּלוֹ אֵת בְּשַׂר עָרְלָתוֹ
Ve'Avraham ben-tish'im vatésha shanah, behimmolo et besar orlato.
Literally, Abraham was ninety-nine years old when he was circumcised in the flesh of his foreskin.
The Hebrew root מוּל (mul) means to circumcise. In this passage, it describes an actual physical act, not merely a symbolic emotional experience.
But its covenant significance goes much deeper.
In Genesis 17:11, God describes circumcision as an אוֹת בְּרִית (ot berit) — a sign of the covenant.
It was a visible mark of God's covenant with Abraham and his descendants.
Abraham was not purchasing God's favor through physical suffering. He was responding in obedience to the God who had already called him, made promises to him, and counted his faith as righteousness.
That distinction changes everything.
Before Genesis 17, there was Genesis 15:6:
“And he believed in the LORD; and he counted it to him for righteousness.”
Abraham was counted righteous before he was circumcised.
The apostle Paul deliberately emphasizes this in Romans 4:9–12, explaining that circumcision was a sign and seal of the righteousness Abraham had received through faith while still uncircumcised.
Grace preceded the mark.
Faith preceded the outward act.
God's initiative preceded Abraham's response.
And that is where the Gospel begins to confront our religious instincts.

You cannot purchase salvation with your suffering. You cannot earn forgiveness by performing enough religious duties. You cannot make God indebted to you through your generosity, attendance, ministry, or reputation.
Salvation is God's gift through Jesus Christ, received by faith, not something we earn through works (Ephesians 2:8–10).
But genuine faith does not make obedience irrelevant.
It makes obedience a response to grace.
Abraham's story becomes even more extraordinary when you remember what happened before this moment.
This was not the story of a flawless man.

Abraham had experienced fear. He had misrepresented his relationship with Sarah. He and Sarah had attempted to obtain the promised offspring through Hagar, an enslaved Egyptian woman, creating painful consequences within their household.
Ishmael was born.
Years passed.
Abraham had experienced the consequences of human decisions made in the middle of divine promises.
Yet Genesis 17 does not begin with God declaring Abraham beyond redemption.
It begins with God revealing Himself.
“I am the Almighty God; walk before me, and be thou perfect.” — Genesis 17:1
In Hebrew, God identifies Himself as אֵל שַׁדַּי (El Shaddai), traditionally translated as God Almighty.
The word translated as “perfect” is תָמִים (tamim), carrying the sense of completeness, integrity, or blamelessness.
God was calling Abraham to walk before Him with integrity and wholehearted devotion.
Not because Abraham had never failed.
But because his failures did not excuse him from the call to faithfulness.
Someone reading this needs to understand that.
Your history may explain your struggle, but it does not have to determine your future.
You may have wasted years.
You may have disappointed people who trusted you.
You may have made decisions that still keep you awake at night.
You may have walked away from God so many times that you are embarrassed to return.
But the Gospel does not announce that redemption is available only to people who managed to get everything right early in life.
Jesus Christ came to save sinners.
And repentance is not pretending your past never happened. It is turning away from sin and returning to God, trusting His mercy rather than defending your rebellion.
Abraham could not undo every decision he had made.
But he could obey God that day.
And so can you.
Notice something easily overlooked in Genesis 17:26.
בְּעֶצֶם הַיּוֹם הַזֶּה (be'etsem hayom hazeh)
On that very day.
Abraham did not wait for a more convenient season. Scripture records that he carried out God's command that very day.
How many times have we promised God a tomorrow that never came?
Tomorrow, I will pray again.
Tomorrow, I will stop returning to that sin.
Tomorrow, I will apologize.
Tomorrow, I will forgive.
Tomorrow, I will open my Bible.
Tomorrow, I will finally take my relationship with Jesus seriously.
And somehow, tomorrow becomes another week.
Another month.
Another year.
Until we wake up and realize that we have spent a significant portion of our lives negotiating with something God has already told us to surrender.
Delayed obedience can become a comfortable disguise for resistance.
Perhaps the most dangerous thing about spiritual complacency is that it rarely announces itself as rebellion.
Sometimes it sounds like, “Not yet.”
But what if today is the day you stop hiding?
What if today is the day you finally confess what you have been protecting?
What if today is the day you stop asking God to accommodate the very sin from which Christ came to redeem you?
You do not need to expose your private struggles publicly. God already knows them. But those simple words may become an encouragement to another person who feels alone in the same battle.
There is something else remarkable about this passage.
Ishmael was thirteen years old.
Abraham was ninety-nine.
Both received the covenant sign on the same day, along with the males of Abraham's household.
The obedience described in this passage extended beyond Abraham himself.
While God specifically established the covenant line through Isaac, He also heard Abraham's concern for Ishmael and promised to bless him (Genesis 17:18–21).
Ishmael was not forgotten.
And although we must not confuse the ancient household structure with modern Christian discipleship, the passage reminds us that our response to God can profoundly affect the people around us.
Your children may remember more about how you lived than what you preached.
Your family may learn something about repentance by watching you admit that you were wrong.
Your friends may begin to understand grace when they see you forgive someone who hurt you.
Your spouse may witness the transforming work of Christ when you stop defending your pride and begin practicing humility.
Sometimes the most powerful sermon your family will ever hear is the sound of you saying, “I was wrong. Please forgive me.”
That is not weakness.
That is what the fruit of repentance can look like.
But we must understand Genesis 17 through the fullness of Scripture.
Christians are not required to undergo physical circumcision to receive salvation or become members of God's people through Christ.
The apostles addressed this directly in Acts 15, rejecting the demand that Gentile believers must be circumcised to be saved.
Paul writes in Galatians 5:6 that what matters in Christ Jesus is faith working through love.
The deeper biblical theme is the transformation of the heart.
Deuteronomy 10:16 speaks of circumcising the heart and abandoning stubbornness.
Deuteronomy 30:6 goes further, promising that God Himself will circumcise the hearts of His people so that they may love Him.
In Romans 2:29, Paul uses the Greek expression:
περιτομὴ καρδίας ἐν πνεύματι (peritomē kardias en pneumati)
Circumcision of the heart, by the Spirit.
And Colossians 2:11 speaks of:
περιτομῇ ἀχειροποιήτῳ (peritomē acheiropoiētō)
A circumcision made without hands.
Paul connects this spiritual reality to our union with Christ, His death and resurrection, and the forgiveness of our trespasses (Colossians 2:11–14).
What human hands cannot accomplish within the depths of your soul, God can accomplish through His redeeming work in Christ.
Christianity is not merely behavior modification.
It is not putting religious clothing over an unchanged heart.
It is not learning how to appear righteous while privately nurturing everything that contradicts the character of Jesus.
It is new life through Christ.
And sometimes that transformation confronts the things we have spent our entire lives protecting.
The ego.
The lust.
The greed.
The resentment.
The need to control everything.
The desperate hunger for approval.
The secret belief that we can save ourselves.
God's sanctifying work may be uncomfortable because repentance involves turning away from things we have grown attached to.
But discomfort itself is not proof of God's work, and suffering does not purchase His love.
At Calvary, Jesus Christ bore our sins.
He was wounded for our transgressions. He died for our sins and rose again, conquering death.
The foundation of our redemption is not what we cut away from ourselves.
It is what Jesus accomplished for us.
The cross is where our self-righteousness loses its argument.
It is where the guilty discover mercy.
Where the ashamed discover that forgiveness is possible.
Where sinners discover that their worst chapter does not have to become their eternal identity.
This is why Gospel Warrior carries the message:
Not because sin is insignificant.
But because the sacrifice of Jesus Christ is sufficient.
Not because our choices have no consequences.
But because our failures are not greater than His redeeming power.
Not because grace gives us permission to remain unchanged.
But because grace teaches us to renounce ungodliness and live faithfully before God (Titus 2:11–14).
Maybe you are twenty-five and already feel like you have ruined your life.
Maybe you are forty-five and secretly grieving the person you could have become.
Maybe you are sixty, seventy, or eighty, wondering whether there is anything meaningful left for you to do.
Remember Abraham.
Ninety-nine years old.
Still being called to obedience.
Still walking with God.
Still awaiting the fulfillment of a promise.
Your age does not place you beyond God's call to repentance, faithfulness, and spiritual growth.
You may not receive the same earthly promises Abraham received, but every believer can rest in the faithfulness of the same God.
Do not confuse the passing of years with the expiration of grace.
And please, do not mistake God's patience for permission to keep postponing repentance.
Behind every article is a mission to bring biblical truth into places where people are struggling, searching, grieving, and desperately needing the hope found in Jesus Christ.
Scripture teaches:
“Every man according as he purposeth in his heart, so let him give; not grudgingly, or of necessity: for God loveth a cheerful giver.” — 2 Corinthians 9:7
Supporting Gospel-centered ministry can be one meaningful way to glorify God through the stewardship of what He has entrusted to you.
You are choosing, if you are willing and able, to help make biblical nourishment available to more people.
Never underestimate what God can accomplish through faithful acts of generosity, service, and encouragement.
Before you leave, ask yourself one final question.
What am I still holding onto that I know does not belong in a life surrendered to Jesus?
Do not answer according to what people expect from you.
Answer before God.
He knows the history behind your hesitation. He knows the wounds behind your walls. He knows the sins behind your carefully maintained reputation.
And the Gospel calls you to stop hiding and come to Christ.
You cannot rewrite yesterday.
You cannot recover every wasted opportunity.
You cannot erase every consequence of your decisions.
But through Jesus Christ, you can receive forgiveness, walk in newness of life, and begin obeying God today.
Abraham was ninety-nine when he received the covenant sign.
Whatever your age, whatever your history, whatever chapter you find yourself in, do not spend another year defending what Scripture calls you to surrender.
Come to Jesus.
Not when you have perfected yourself.
Not when you have repaired every broken piece.
Come in repentance and faith, trusting the One whose death and resurrection are sufficient for your salvation.
The years you have spent running from God do not have to become the years you spend dying far from Him.
Your past may explain the scars, but it does not have the final authority over a life redeemed by Jesus Christ.
